procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment dated 7th July, 2016 of High Court of Judicature at Bombay in Writ Petition No.1550 of 2016
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The appellant (daughter-in-law) filed a writ petition in the High Court of Judicature at Bombay (Writ Petition No. 1550 of 2016) challenging the order of 5th Additional Judge, Small Causes Court dated 5th November, 2014 and the order passed by the District Judge, Pune dated 17th December, 2015. The High Court dismissed the writ petition, holding that the Small Causes Court cannot entertain the counter claim due to Section 15 and the Second Schedule of Act, 1887.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant (daughter-in-law), aggrieved by the High Court's order, appealed to the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, setting aside the judgments of the High Court, District Judge, and Small Causes Court. The Supreme Court held that the counter claim filed by the appellant is fully entertainable by the Judge, Small Causes Court.

directions: The judgment of the High Court dated 07.07.2016, judgment and order dated 05.11.2014 of 5•h Additional Judge, Small Causes Court, Pune and judgment dated 17.12.2015 of the District Judge, Pune are set aside.
It is held that counter claim filed by the appellant in Civil Suit No. 77of2013 is fully entertainable by Judge, Small Causes Court and needs to be considered in accordance with law.

issue.issue_text: Whether the Small Causes Court has the jurisdiction to entertain a counterclaim filed by the appellant seeking an order of residence.

facts: A father-in-law filed a suit in the Small Causes Court to remove his daughter-in-law (the appellant) from a flat, claiming she was a 'gratuitous licensee'.
The daughter-in-law filed a counterclaim in the same suit.
In her counterclaim, she sought an 'order of residence' in the flat, a right available to her under Section 19 of the Domestic Violence Act, 2005 (Act, 2005).
law: The lower courts (Small Causes Court, District Judge, and High Court) relied on Section 15 and the Second Schedule of the Provincial Small Cause Courts Act, 1887, which generally bars the court from deciding issues related to rights or interests in immovable property.

The Supreme Court focused on Section 26 of the Domestic Violence Act, 2005. This section allows an aggrieved person to seek reliefs available under the Act (such as the right of residence) in 'any legal proceeding' before a civil court, family court, or criminal court.
application: The Supreme Court reasoned that the suit filed by the father-in-law in the Small Causes Court qualified as a 'legal proceeding' before a 'Civil court'.
Therefore, under the specific provision of Section 26 of the 2005 Act, the daughter-in-law was entitled to seek the relief of residence in that very proceeding.
The Court found that the daughter-in-law's claim for a right of residence was 'inter-connected' with the father-in-law's suit to remove her from the property.

It concluded that refusing to hear the counterclaim would deny the daughter-in-law a right explicitly granted by the 2005 Act and would lead to a 'multiplicity of proceedings', which is contrary to the purpose of that Act.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court held that the Small Causes Court had the jurisdiction to entertain the counterclaim. It set aside the lower courts' orders and ruled that the counterclaim was 'fully entertainable' and should be considered on its merits.

issue.issue_text: Whether substantive issues can be decided by a Judge, Small Causes Court.

facts: The case involved a proceeding before a Judge, Small Causes Court.
A party in this proceeding sought to claim reliefs available under a different law, specifically Sections 18 to 22 of an act referred to as "Act, 2005".
The opposing party argued that a Small Causes Court has limited jurisdiction and cannot decide substantive issues, citing the limited applicability of the Civil Procedure Code.
law: A proceeding before a Judge, Small Causes Court is considered a "legal proceeding".
A Judge, Small Causes Court is considered a "civil court".
Section 26 of the "Act, 2005" allows an aggrieved person to seek reliefs available under Sections 18 to 22 of that Act in any legal proceeding before a civil court.
application: The Supreme Court established that a Small Causes Court is fundamentally a "civil court" and the matters before it are "legal proceedings".
The Court then applied the rule from Section 26 of the "Act, 2005". This section broadly permits certain reliefs to be sought in *any* legal proceeding before a civil court.

By connecting these two points, the Court reasoned that since a case in a Small Causes Court is a "legal proceeding" before a "civil court", it is a valid forum for an aggrieved person to seek the substantive reliefs provided under the 2005 Act.
Therefore, the specific provision of Section 26 grants the Small Causes Court the jurisdiction to entertain and decide on these substantive issues, notwithstanding its otherwise limited jurisdiction.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that a Judge, Small Causes Court can decide substantive issues because it qualifies as a "civil court" conducting a "legal proceeding". Therefore, under specific statutory provisions like Section 26 of the "Act, 2005", it has the jurisdiction to grant substantive reliefs available under that Act.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the Small Causes Court has the jurisdiction to entertain a counterclaim filed by the appellant seeking an order of residence.
appellant_arguments: The counterclaim filed in the Small Causes Court seeking an order of residence was fully entertainable and should be considered.
The appellant's position is supported by a judgment of the Bombay High Court in Ambreen Aklroon vs. Aditya Aurn Paudwal.
respondent_arguments: The Small Causes Court does not have the jurisdiction to entertain the appellant's counterclaim for an order of residence.

arguments.issue_text: Whether substantive issues can be decided by a Judge, Small Causes Court.
appellant_arguments: A Judge of the Small Causes Court can decide substantive issues when they are raised in a counterclaim that is otherwise entertainable by the court.
respondent_arguments: A Judge of the Small Causes Court cannot decide substantive issues, as its jurisdiction is limited.

cases.case_name: Union of India and another v. G.M. Kokil and others
cases.principle: A statutory provision containing a non obstante clause has to be given full effect.

cases.case_name: Hirai P. Harsora and others v. Kusum Narottamdas Harsora and others
cases.principle: The text states this case was 'relied on' but does not specify the legal principle for which it was cited.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: Reliefs available under the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005 can be sought in any legal proceeding before a civil court. Given the Act's social purpose, its provisions, particularly Section 26, must be construed widely. A civil court is not barred from considering a claim under the Act unless such a bar is expressly provided by statute.
obiter: In a conflict between a general statute and a special statute, the special statute will have an overriding effect.
A statutory provision containing a non-obstante clause must be given its full effect.
If two special statutes are in conflict, the one enacted later in time will override the earlier one.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court found that a counterclaim seeking relief under the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005, is fully entertainable in a suit before the Small Causes Court. This is because Section 26 of the 2005 Act, a special social welfare law, must be interpreted broadly to effectuate its purpose. Unless a civil court's jurisdiction to hear such a claim is expressly barred, the court should not infer a bar, especially when the claim is interconnected with the main suit and hearing it would prevent a multiplicity of proceedings.
legal_tests_applied: Social purpose legislation, like the 2005 Act, must be construed widely to effectuate its very purpose and object.
Unless the determination of a claim under the 2005 Act is expressly barred from consideration by a civil court, a court should be loath to read in a bar to its consideration in any legal proceeding.
A statutory provision containing a non-obstante clause has to be given full effect.
The 2005 Act, being a special law, must be given full effect.
policy_considerations: The 2005 Act was enacted to secure a social purpose.
Denial of consideration of the counter-claim would lead to multiplicity of proceedings, which cannot be the object and purpose of the 2005 Act.
The right of residence claimed by the appellant in her counter-claim is inter-connected with the determination of the issue in the suit filed before the civil court.
Denial of consideration of the counter-claim shall amount to denial of consideration of the claim as contemplated by s.26 of the 2005 Act.
